title: I've been to Denmark
goal: Form the present perfect ("have done") with *har* and *er*, and know when to use which.
bekal: form the present perfect: *har* + past participle
choose between *har* and *er* — and see why it isn't blind memorization
know when to use the simple past and when to use the present perfect
wave: Review **unit 17** first: tell the story of yesterday in ten past-tense sentences, linked with *først*, *så*, *bagefter*, *til sidst*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Har du prøvet det?
dialogs.intro: An evening at Mette's apartment. The three of them are planning their summer vacation.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.id: Have you two been to Jutland?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Jeg har boet i Aarhus i to år, så ja.
lines.id: I've lived in Aarhus for two years, so yes.
lines.literal: I have lived in Aarhus in two years, so yes.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg har aldrig været uden for Sjælland.
lines.literal: I have never been outside for Zealand.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Aldrig? Du har boet her i halvandet år!
lines.id: Never? You've lived here for a year and a half!
lines.literal: never? you have lived here in half-second year!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg ved det. Jeg er ikke kommet ret langt.
lines.id: I know. I haven't gotten very far.
lines.literal: I know it. I am not come rather far.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Så skal du med i sommer. Har du set Skagen?
lines.id: Then you're coming with us this summer. Have you seen Skagen?
lines.literal: then shall you with in summer. have you seen Skagen?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nej. Hvad er der i Skagen?
lines.literal: no. what is there in Skagen?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: To have mødes der. Man kan se linjen i vandet.
lines.id: Two seas meet there. You can see the line in the water.
lines.literal: two seas meet there. one can see line-the in water-the.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Det har jeg aldrig hørt om.
lines.literal: that have I never heard about.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Og har du smagt rigtig dansk sommermad? Nye kartofler og sild?
lines.id: And have you tasted real Danish summer food? New potatoes and herring?
lines.literal: and have you tasted real Danish summer-food? new potatoes and herring?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg har prøvet sild én gang. Det var… en oplevelse.
lines.id: I've tried herring once. It was… an experience.
lines.literal: I have tried herring one time. it was… an experience.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Så er du blevet halvt dansk. Resten kommer af sig selv.
lines.id: Then you've become half Danish. The rest will come by itself.
lines.literal: then are you become half Danish. rest-the comes of itself.

notes: **Har været, har boet, har set** — the present perfect is used for experiences **when no time is mentioned**. *Har du været i Jylland?* asks whether you've ever been, not when.
**Jeg er ikke kommet** — notice *er*, not *har*. *At komme* is a verb of movement, and that group uses *er*. The rule is below.
**Halvandet** = one and a half. A single word for 1½ — English has nothing this compact. The et-form is *halvandet*, the en-form *halvanden*: *halvanden time* (an hour and a half), *halvandet år*.
**Ret langt** — *ret* here means "rather, very", not "right". *Ikke ret langt* = not very far. One of those words whose meaning shifts with its position.

**Det har jeg aldrig hørt om** — notice the order. *Det* in first place, *har* in second, the subject jumps. The rule from unit 10 still applies unchanged, and the participle (*hørt*) gets thrown to the end.

**To have** = two seas — the plural of *et hav*. At Skagen, the Skagerrak and the Kattegat meet, and the difference in water color is really visible. It's one of the places Danes most often recommend to newcomers.
**Sild** (pickled herring) is the second Danish culture test after lakrids. Budi's reaction — "an experience" — is a very subtle Danish way of saying he didn't like it.
**Af sig selv** = by itself. A fixed phrase; notice the reflexive *sig* from unit 9 showing up again.

grammars.title: Forming the present perfect
body: The structure: **har** or **er** + past participle. For regular verbs, the participle is easy to guess from the past form.
after: The rule is tidy: **-ede → -et**, and **-te → -t**. If you know the past form, you know the participle.

Irregular verbs have to be memorized, but you already have the list — the fourth column of the big table in unit 18. Most end in *-et*: *taget*, *fået*, *givet*, *fundet*, *drukket*. Some are short: *set*, *sagt*, *gjort*, *haft*, *været*.

grammars.title: Har or er?
body: The choice isn't blind memorization — there's logic behind it, and once you see it, you'll rarely get it wrong.
**er** is used when the focus is on the **result of a movement or change of state**. **har** is used for everything else, including the activity itself.

head: With er
Meaning
With har
Meaning
rows: I've been walking for two hours.
He's been running for an hour.

after: Notice that the left and right columns use **the same verb** with a shifted meaning: left stresses the result (where he is now), right stresses the activity (how long, how much).
The verbs that most often take *er*: **at gå, at komme, at rejse, at blive, at flytte, at ankomme, at dø, at falde, at løbe**. The list is short; everything else takes *har*.
⚠️ *At være* itself takes *har*: *jeg **har** været i Danmark*. This seems to go against the logic, and you simply have to learn it as is.

grammars.title: Simple past or present perfect?
body: The two forms can't be swapped, and the rule is basically the same as in English.

head: Use
When
Example
rows: Jeg **har boet** her i to år.

after: The quick test: **if there's a finished past time expression — *i går*, *i sidste uge*, *klokken to* — use the simple past.** If there isn't, it's almost always the present perfect.
*Jeg har set filmen i går* is wrong, because *i går* is a finished time. It has to be *jeg så filmen i går*. Exactly the same mistake as "I have seen the film yesterday" in English.
The fourth row matters: *jeg har boet her i to år* means I still live here — just like English "I've lived here for two years". If you've moved away, it's *jeg boede her i to år*.

head: Dansk
English
rows: Har du været i Danmark før?
Have you been to Denmark before?
Jeg har boet her i to år.
I've lived here for two years.
Have you ever seen the northern lights?
We've known each other for a long time.

blocks.text: *Endnu* = yet, still. *Ikke endnu* = not yet. There's also *stadig* (still): *Han er stadig her.*
*Jeg har lige spist* — *lige* here means "just now", not "quickly" as in unit 13. The same word with two jobs, told apart by its position.
The present perfect is the form for talking about experiences — what you have and haven't done. It's the most common conversation material when you meet new people.

head: Frame
Example
rows: Jeg har aldrig set sne før.
Jeg har prøvet at lave dansk mad.
Jeg har ikke set Skagen endnu.
Hvor længe har du boet i Danmark?

blocks.title: Three things you may never have done in Denmark
items: *Jeg har aldrig svømmet i havet i maj.* Danes do it. The water is about ten degrees, and they call it refreshing.
*Jeg har aldrig været til en julefrokost.* The Danish office Christmas lunch is a social institution of its own, lasting from noon until late, and people talk about it for months afterwards.
*Jeg har aldrig cyklet i sne.* That will change. Danish cities clear the bike lanes before they clear the roads.

blocks.text: Notice that *aldrig*, *allerede* and *lige* stand between the helper verb and the participle: *jeg har **aldrig** set*, *jeg har **allerede** spist*. Same spot as *ikke* — the rule from unit 10 reused unchanged.
